title: Chapter 2: Rebirth
content:
Chapter 2

The very second Wei Wuxian opened his eyes, a solid kick slammed into his ribs.

A voice detonated over him like a crack of thunder: “Stop playing dead, you freak!”

The blow nearly made him cough up a lung. His head bounced off the dirt floor, leaving him staring dumbly at the rafters. Through the haze in his skull, one distinct thought surfaced:Kicking the Patriarch himself? Someone’s feeling suicidal today.

It had been so many years since he’d heard a living voice that the shrill yelling made his ears ring and his vision blur. A young guy with a grating, puberty-cracked voice kept screeching through the buzz: “Did you forget whose land you’re living on? Whose rice you’re shoveling down your throat? Whose money keeps you alive? So what if I took a few of your trinkets? They should’ve been mine to begin with!”

Cue the clatter and crash of someone violently ransacking the room. Drawers were yanked, jars were smashed, and furniture was shoved around with reckless abandon. Slowly, Wei Wuxian’s eyes focused. Above him hung a dingy, cobwebbed ceiling—and hovering right in his field of view was a twisted face with beady, venomous eyes, spraying spit with every syllable: “You actually had the nerve to tattle on me! Think I’m scared? You really think anyone under this roof gives a damn about you?”

A couple of burly servants lumbered into view. “Young Master, we smashed the lot!”

The rasping teenager frowned. “Already? That was fast.”

“Well, it’s a dump,” one servant scoffed. “Wasn't much in here to begin with.”

Evidently satisfied, the boy rounded on Wei Wuxian again. He jabbed a finger so close Wei Wuxian thought his nose was about to get shoved into his brain. “You had the guts to run your mouth to my parents, so why play dead now? As if anyone cares about your stash of scrap metal and scrap paper! Well, I’ve trashed it all. Let's see you try to complain now! So you spent a few years playing disciple at some fancy sect—think you’re hot shit? You still got kicked to the curb and dragged your tail home like a beaten stray!”

Wei Wuxian lay there, half-dead, thinking:

First off, I've been dead for years. Not playing.

Second: who the hell are you?

Third: where the hell am I??

And fourth… when on earth did I ever sign up to snatch a body?!

Having thoroughly vented his rage with kicks and vandalism, the shrill teenager swaggered out the door flanked by his two thugs. He slammed the door behind him and barked, “Keep an eye on him! Don’t let him out to embarrass the family!”

“Right away, Young Master!” the guards chorused.

Once the footsteps faded, the room sank into absolute silence. Wei Wuxian tried to push himself up, but his limbs completely refused to cooperate, dropping him flat on his back again. Giving up on sitting, he rolled over to take in the unfamiliar room and the wreckage strewn across the floor, his head still pounding.

A brass mirror lay discarded in the debris nearby. He reached out, grabbed it, and pulled it up to his face.

Staring back from the bronze surface was an unnervingly chalk-white face, flanked by two lopsided, clumpy splotches of bright rouge on either cheek. Stick a long red tongue out of that mug, and you’d have a textbook hanging ghost.

Horrified, Wei Wuxian flung the mirror away. He wiped a sleeve across his cheek, coming away with a palm caked in thick white powder.

Small mercies: this body didn’t naturally look like a sleep paralysis demon; it just had atrocious taste. A grown man caked in enough cheap cosmetic plaster to look like a poorly painted wall—and applied with zero artistic skill, to boot.

The shock gave him just enough adrenaline to haul himself into a seated position. Only then did he notice the circular ritual array drawn beneath him.

The circle was sloppy, warped, and painted a stark, glistening crimson. It smelled strongly of iron—drawn by hand in fresh blood. Inside the border ran jagged, frantic runes, slightly smeared where his body had shifted over them. The remnants radiated a raw, unmistakably sinister energy. Wei Wuxian hadn’t spent lifetimes being hailed as the Supreme Fiend and the Grandmaster of Demonic Cultivation for nothing; he took one glance at the array and knew precisely what foul business he was looking at.

He hadn’t stolen this body.

He had been offered it.

Sacrificial Summoning.

At its core, it was a self-mutilating curse. The caster cuts themselves with a blade, using their own blood to inscribe the circle and incantations. Sitting at the center, they offer their mortal vessel to an evil spirit in exchange for their own soul being cast into the earth, summoning a vile, irredeemable fiend to fulfill whatever wish they died harboring. It was the exact opposite of forcibly possessing someone else's flesh. Both were taboo, forbidden arts, but this ritual was far less practical and infinitely less popular. Very few people ever harbored hatred so absolute that they would willingly destroy their own souls for it. Over centuries, the technique had practically vanished into myth. Across historical records, barely three or four cases had ever been verified, and in every single instance, the caster’s wish had been bloody, merciless revenge—which the summoned fiends carried out down to the gruesome letter.

Wei Wuxian felt deeply offended.

Since when was he classified as a “vile, irredeemable fiend”?

Sure, his reputation was trash, and fine, his death had been gory beyond belief, but he hadn't haunted a single person, nor had he sought revenge! He was willing to swear to the heavens that you couldn't find a more law-abiding, well-behaved stray phantom in the entire underworld!

The real problem was that the sacrificial pact was entirely dictated by the summoner’s intent. No matter how unfair it felt… his soul was already locked into the flesh. The contract was signed in blood. Hehadto fulfill the caster's wish, or the curse would backfire violently, obliterating his soul so completely he’d never reincarnate.

Wei Wuxian ripped open his robe and held up his arms. Sure enough, deep, jagged crisscrosses carved by a blade scored both of his forearms. Though the bleeding had stopped, he knew these cuts weren't normal wounds. Until the summoner’s vengeance was satisfied, they would never heal. And if he took too long, the curse would tear his newly claimed body and soul into bloody ribbons.

After confirming the dreadful reality of his situation, Wei Wuxian mentally hurled about ten string of curses at the ceiling before dragging himself to his feet against the wall.

The room was spacious enough, but barren, cold, and utterly destitute. The bed quilt looked like it hadn't met a washbasin in months, reeking of damp mildew. Over in the corner, a wicker wastebasket had been kicked on its side, dumping trash and crumpled paper across the floorboards. Spotting ink on one of the wads, Wei Wuxian picked it up and smoothed it out. Dense, erratic scrawls covered the surface. He immediately began gathering up the rest of the crumpled balls.

The writing was clearly the previous owner’s desperate ventings during bouts of deep anguish. Sections were frantic and incoherent, the frantic pressure of the brush screaming pure anxiety. Wei Wuxian forced himself to read through them piece by piece, his brow furrowing deeper with every line. Something was very wrong here.

Piecing together the fragments, he managed to assemble a rough picture.

First off: the vessel's name was Mo Xuanyu, and this place was Mo Village.

Mo Xuanyu’s maternal grandfather had been the local squire—wealthy, but cursed with a thin bloodline. Despite his best efforts, he only ever sired two daughters. The papers didn't name them, but the eldest was born of the legitimate wife and took in a husband to carry the family name. The second daughter was breathtakingly gorgeous, but born to a housemaid. The family had planned to marry her off cheaply to some commoner, but fate had other plans: when she was sixteen, the leader of a prominent cultivation sect passed through the town and was struck by her beauty. Mo Village became their secret rendezvous spot, and a year later, the second daughter gave birth to a boy—Mo Xuanyu.

At first, the locals sneered at the scandalous affair. But in this era, commoners virtually worshipped cultivators; the great clans were seen as divine beings blessed by heaven, untouchable and aristocratic. When the sect leader started showering the second daughter's household with gifts and favor, the town did an immediate about-face. Suddenly, the Mo clan treated it as their greatest honor, and the townsfolk practically choked on envy.

The good times didn't last. The sect leader was merely chasing a fleeting thrill; after a couple of years, the novelty wore off and the visits dwindled. By the time Mo Xuanyu turned four, his father stopped coming altogether.

Inevitably, the village gossip shifted back. The old sneers returned, now spiced with condescending pity. Second Lady Mo refused to accept reality, stubbornly clinging to the belief that a great sect leader would never abandon his own flesh and blood. And she was proven right: when Mo Xuanyu turned fourteen, the sect leader sent a grand retinue to formally escort the boy to his clan.

Second Lady Mo’s head shot right back up. Even though she wasn't allowed to tag along, all her past humiliation evaporated. She went around bragging to anyone who would listen that her son was bound to become the Chief Cultivator, bring boundless glory to the ancestors, and stand above all men. Once again, the Mo Village wind changed direction.

Yet, before Mo Xuanyu could achieve greatness or inherit a sliver of his father’s legacy, he was kicked out.

And not just dismissed—he was thrown out in utter disgrace. Turns out, Mo Xuanyu was a cutsleeve. Worse, he’d had the audacity to harass and pursue a fellow male disciple. The scandal broke wide open for everyone to see. Add to that his thoroughly mediocre talent and stalled cultivation, and the sect had zero reason to keep him around.

To make matters worse, whatever trauma he endured broke him. He returned home utterly unhinged, unstable and erratic, like a frightened animal whose wits had been permanently scrambled.

Reading this, Wei Wuxian’s eyebrows twitched.

A cutsleeve is one thing, but a lunatic too?No wonder his face was painted like a corpse bride, and no wonder nobody batted an eye at the bloody occult circle covering the floor. If Mo Xuanyu had smeared blood across the floor, walls, and ceiling, the servants probably would have just shrugged. Everyone simply assumed he was out of his mind!

After his disgraceful return, the mockery was relentless, and this time, there was no bouncing back. Second Lady Mo couldn't stomach the humiliation; suffocating on her own bitter fury, she literally dropped dead from rage.

By then, the old patriarch had passed away, leaving the eldest sister in charge of the estate. The First Madam Mo had hated her half-sister since childhood, and she directed all that venom straight onto the illegitimate nephew. She had only one precious son—the screeching brat who had just trashed the room, Mo Ziyuan. Back when Mo Xuanyu was being escorted away in glory, Madam Mo assumed their connection to an immortal sect meant they could ride the coattails, expecting the envoys to pack Mo Ziyuan along for cultivation training, too. Naturally, the envoys had flatly ignored the absurd request.

What a joke. Cultivation training wasn't like buying cabbages at the market—there was no 'buy one, get one free'!

Yet somehow, the family suffered from a staggering delusion: they were thoroughly convinced Mo Ziyuan had natural spiritual talent, and that ifhehad been chosen, the immortals would have adored him instead of letting him turn out to be a useless disappointment like his cousin. Mo Ziyuan had grown up spoon-fed these bitter delusions until he believed them implicitly. He took every opportunity to torment Mo Xuanyu, accusing him of stealing his path to immortality. At the same time, he treated Mo Xuanyu's leftover sect relics—talismans, elixirs, minor spiritual tools—like his personal toybox, pawning and breaking whatever caught his eye. Though half-mad, Mo Xuanyu wasn't completely oblivious to the abuse. He endured it as long as he could, but Mo Ziyuan grew greedier by the day, practically gutting his quarters. Driven to the brink, Mo Xuanyu finally stammered out a complaint to his aunt and uncle.

And so, Mo Ziyuan had come kicking down the door for payback today.

The handwriting on the scraps was tiny and cramped, making Wei Wuxian’s eyes ache.What a miserable, hellish existence.No wonder Mo Xuanyu was willing to sacrifice his own soul just to drag a vengeful spirit down to clean house.

Once his eyes stopped aching, his head started throbbing again. Normally, when the array is cast, the summoner silently recites their demands so the arriving evil spirit knows what to do. But Mo Xuanyu had likely copied this forbidden ritual from an incomplete manuscript, completely botching that crucial step. Wei Wuxian could gather that the boy wanted revenge against the Mo family, but to what extent? What were the terms? Take his stolen things back? Beat the family black and blue?

Or… wipe them all out?

It was probably a massacre, wasn't it? After all, anyone who knew anything about the cultivation world knew the labels slapped onto Wei Wuxian: treacherous, ingrate, lunatic, monster. Who fit the description of an unforgiving evil god better than him? If Mo Xuanyu had specifically called on his name, he wasn't looking for a light tap on the wrist.

Wei Wuxian let out a helpless sigh. “Buddy… you really summoned the wrong guy.”
